paper_title: Accelerate Bench: Evaluating Agents for Application-Level Program Optimization

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Application optimization requires coding agents to discover useful changes and coordinate them across a complete program while preserving the required computation. We introduce Accelerate Bench, a benchmark of 32 CPU optimization tasks adapted from scientific applications and supercomputing competitions. Each task provides a working program and specifies the workload, correctness requirements, timing boundaries, and permitted edits, leaving agents to choose where and how to optimize. Public testing supports iterative development, and a separate verifier scores the final submission. On benchmark version 1.1, we evaluate 16 coding agents, each pairing a model with a harness. Their Score@1 ranges from 25.5% to 67.4%. Most of their programs are correct, and the size of the speedup separates them: the two leading agents are at least 2x faster on 22 or more of the 32 tasks, while the other fourteen reach 2x on 8 to 17 and leave 125 of their 412 correct outcomes below 1.25x. Controlled replays show why coordination across an application matters: identical source code runs between 0.29x and 2.12x depending only on build and runtime settings, and one code change is worth 1.01x or 6.4x depending on another. Accelerate Bench pairs executable workloads with agents' programs and trajectories to evaluate both their gains and the process behind them.

Introduction Software performance engineering improves application performance by identifying and addressing inefficiencies in software and the way it executes (Woodside et al., 2007; Leiserson et al., 2020). Effective optimization often requires interventions across multiple layers of the software stack, from compiler and build configurations to algorithms, data structures, dependencies, and hardware parallelism (Leiserson et al., 2020; Balaprakash et al., 2018). For an existing application, this is typically an iterative engineering process: measuring execution, locating performance bottlenecks, implementing targeted changes, and evaluating their end-to-end impact while preserving correctness (Woodside et al., 2007; Balaprakash et al., 2018). Application-level optimization therefore extends beyond localized code editing. valid patch may leave end-to-end runtime unchanged, and effective speedups can depend on interactions among changes made across different layers of the software stack. Success requires discovering where performance is lost, deciding where to intervene, and verifying that the resulting program is both correct and faster at the workload level. Coding agents offer path toward automating this process. Existing benchmarks such as SWE-Perf, 1 Accelerate Bench: Application-Level Program Optimization Figure 1 Application performance engineering in Accelerate Bench. Left: GSO derives optimization tasks and reference patches from human commits (Shetty et al., 2025). Right: Accelerate Bench defines tasks by an application and its workload, illustrated with SU2 . Compile time is reported separately and excluded from reward; Agent time covers the agent-execution phase. The diagnostic displays illustrate the tools used in this workflow. GSO, and SWE-fficiency evaluate performance optimization in real software repositories using tasks derived from human optimization commits or pull requests (He et al., 2026; Shetty et al., 2025; Ma et al., 2026). These benchmarks anchor evaluation around known optimization instances, providing realistic repositories and expert optimization references. We study complementary setting: can an agent optimize an application when the required behavior and workload are specified, but no known optimization patch determines where or how the agent should intervene? Inspired by behavioral specification in ProgramBench (Yang et al., 2026), we define optimization tasks by the computation that must be preserved and the workload that must become faster. Within permitted edit scope, the agent may modify algorithms, implementation, build settings, dependencies, and runtime configuration. We introduce Accelerate Bench, benchmark of 32 CPU optimization tasks adapted from scientific applications and supercomputing competition problems. Each task provides working initial program together with correctness requirements, timing boundaries, permitted edits, and public testing interface. Agents iteratively edit, build, execute, and evaluate candidate programs, while separate verifier scores the final submission. This setup requires agents to discover optimization opportunities and convert them into verified end-to-end acceleration. We evaluate 16 coding agents on version 1.1 of Accelerate Bench, comparing correctness and end-to-end acceleration across the 32 tasks. Most of their programs are correct, so correctness alone 2 Accelerate Bench: Application-Level Program Optimization does not separate the agents; the size of the speedup does. The two leading agents are at least 2 faster on 22 or more tasks, whereas the other fourteen reach 2 on 8 to 17 tasks and leave 125 of their 412 correct outcomes below 1.25. Accelerate Bench also records how agents optimize. From annotated trajectories of five agents on benchmark v1.0 and controlled replays of their programs, we ask what changes agents make to an application, how they test and develop candidate programs, and how optimization choices interact; the analysis characterizes optimization on these tasks rather than explaining the v1.1 ranking. Our contributions are: workload-defined optimization benchmark. Each of the 32 tasks fixes the computation, complete outputs, stateful checks such as checkpoint recovery, and timing boundaries; public tests support iteration, and private verifier scores the final submission. In 14 planned controls on two tasks, every valid variant passes and all eight invalid variants fail the check they violate (Section 2). An evaluation of 16 coding agents on benchmark v1.1. Correctness alone does not separate the agents: each is correct on 26 to 32 of the 32 tasks, while Score@1 ranges from 25.5% to 67.4% and the number of tasks with at least 2 speedup from 8 to 23 (Section 4). An analysis of how agents optimize. From 480 runs of five agents on benchmark v1.0 and controlled replays of their programs, we find that these agents mostly change the computation and rarely the build, although build and runtime settings alone move one unchanged GROMACS program between 0.29 and 2.12. Code changes also interact: one change in QiboTN program is worth 1.01 on its own and 6.4 once another change is in place (Section 5). We will release the versioned task packages, including public tests and verifiers. 2. Benchmark Construction Accelerate Bench comprises 32 CPU optimization tasks adapted from mature scientific applications across six established supercomputing competitions. We adapt each task into an executable workload running in resource-constrained environment, with explicit permitted modifications, timing boundaries, and output requirements. We pair interactive public feedback during development with held-out private verification. Experienced finalists of the ASC Student Supercomputer Challenge reviewed the task designs. Appendix D.1 documents task origins and adaptations. 2.1. Task Definition and Optimization Scope Unlike benchmarks built around isolated historical commits or patches (Shetty et al., 2025; He et al., 2026), we define each task by complete application workload and its required outputs. Each task fixes the target computation and leaves agents to decide where and how to optimize. We evaluate performance across the full workflow, so local improvements count only if they reduce total runtime. Each task provides working baseline implementation, build and execution scripts, task instructions, and public testing interface in container with fixed CPU core and memory limits (Appendix D). Agents may modify application source code, compiler options, and dependencies within the permitted directory, while preserving the required computations and outputs. Application-level optimization means reducing the end-to-end runtime of this prescribed workflow under these resource limits. Figure 1 illustrates this workflow with SU2 : agents optimize an airfoil flow simulation by editing solver routines, common libraries, and compilation flags. To pass, each run must complete all 250 iterations on the supplied 10,216-element mesh and produce five complete flow-field snapshots. The public test rebuilds the candidate, runs the simulation, and checks field residuals and run-to-run 3 Accelerate Bench: Application-Level Program Optimization Figure 2 Score@1 by application area. Benchmark v1.1, first run of the 16 agents in Table 1; top six agents per area, increasing clockwise. Labels give the top three scores (%); each sector is scaled to its own maximum (dashed arc). The verifier alone controls the validation meshes, physical configurations, and the checking code used to score submissions. Timing boundaries follow each tasks computational workflow, excluding one-time setup and build steps; end-to-end runtime in this paper means this timed workflow, and build time is reported separately. For example, GROMACS times the mdrun simulation, excluding build time and topology preparation; the HPCG-derived task times sparse matrix assembly, initialization, multigrid solves, and output; and paged generation times model loading, autoregressive decoding, checkpoint saving, and recovery in new process. Because these stages are timed and checked together, faster kernel counts only in proportion to its share of the workflow, and shortcut that skips required output or recovery step fails correctness rather than earning speedup. Appendix Table 12 gives representative contracts, and Table 10 lists each tasks CPU cores, memory, and time limits; every task package specifies its own outputs and checks. 2.2. Task Adaptation, Domain Coverage, and Workload Scaling The 32 tasks span eight application areas (Figure 2) curated from six supercomputing competitions: ASC, PAC, the ACM-China International Parallel Computing Challenge (IPCC), SCC at SC and ISC, and IndySCC (Appendix Table 13). Each task adapts competitions target application and optimization challenge into bounded, self-contained workload rather than reproducing the original input (Appendix D.1). Twenty-nine tasks build on the competitions application, from full source trees to selected solver subtrees; three ( Paged LM generation , Tucker reconstruction and Graph sparsification ) are workflows we wrote around competitions optimization theme. We standardize dependencies, build scripts, and execution entry points in isolated containers, using inputs from canonical benchmarks, public datasets, or synthetic generators. 4 Accelerate Bench: Application-Level Program Optimization Workload scaling. Competition workloads typically run on multi-node clusters for hours. To allow agents to iteratively edit, build, and test within practical evaluation budget, we adapt these workloads to single-node CPU environments by reducing input sizes and iteration counts. The adapted tasks retain the main computational stages, inter-stage dependencies, and numerical correctness criteria of the original applications (adaptation parameters in Appendix D.1). Because private inputs are often larger than the public ones (Section 2.3), change that helps only on small inputs earns less. Timing covers the whole workflow, so savings in fixed costs such as process startup and library imports also count. 2.3. Public Tests, Private Verification, and Checks Agents develop against public test; private verifier scores the submission (Figure 1). During the run, the agent can call the public test repeatedly; it rebuilds the current program, runs it on few public inputs (typically two), checks the outputs, and reports correctness, runtime and, in most tasks, the baseline runtime or speedup, or the failing step. The agent sees whether its program builds, produces the required outputs, and runs faster, but not the checking code. After the run, the hidden verifier rebuilds the submitted files and runs them on private inputs of the same kind, typically four. Most tasks include the public inputs and held-out inputs that are often larger or freshly randomized per evaluation, such as other Mach numbers and angles of attack for SU2 . Only the verifiers repeated timings and checks set the reward (Section 3), so the score depends on inputs the agent has not seen. To prevent invalid optimizationssuch as skipping required computations or omitting output fieldsthe verifier enforces correctness checks. Submissions must meet task-specific numerical tolerances, generate complete output files, and satisfy stateful requirements such as recovering correctly from saved checkpoint in new process; only submissions passing all checks are scored on runtime. In 14 planned controls on HPCG-derived and paged generation (Appendix E), every valid variant passes and all eight invalid variants fail the check they violate: omitting the second solution fails the output-size check, and four attention variants that pass component tests fail application checks. 3. Analysis We answer the three questions from Section 1: what changes agents make to an application (Section 5.1), how they test and develop candidate programs (Section 5.2), and how optimization choices 7 Accelerate Bench: Application-Level Program Optimization interact to affect end-to-end performance (Section 5.3). Analysis sample. For this analysis, we run five agents, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, Grok 4.6, DeepSeekV4-Pro, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and Hy3, three times on each task at high reasoning effort, giving 480 runs. trajectory is the complete record of runs messages, tool calls, and outputs; candidate is program the agent sends to the public tests. GPT-5.6 Luna labels the optimization techniques in each runs final submission (476 runs), and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash annotates every tool calls action, reason, and cited feedback, together with the relationships between changes (Appendix I). These runs use benchmark v1.0; the analysis characterizes how agents optimize on these tasks and does not explain differences among the v1.1 agents. Findings on how agents test and develop candidates are illustrative observations: each states the evidence it rests on, and none estimates how often behavior occurs beyond the runs analyzed. 5.1. Related Work Code optimization benchmarks. Earlier benchmarks measure program efficiency at function scale: PIE studies performance-improving edits to competitive-programming solutions, EffiBench, Mercury and ECCO compare the runtime of generated solutions under correctness tests, EvalPerf and ENAMEL add inputs that expose inefficient algorithms and compare against graded or expert references, and ParEval tests whether models write correct parallel code (Shypula et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2024; Du et al., 2024; Waghjale et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024; Qiu et al., 2025; Nichols et al., 2024). SWE-Perf supplies target functions and measures test runtimes; GSO compares repository optimizations with expert implementations; SWE-fficiency asks agents to locate bottlenecks for supplied workload (He et al., 2026; Shetty et al., 2025; Ma et al., 2026). cross-machine replay of their reference patches finds that many tasks do not consistently satisfy the original validity rules (Chen et al., 2026); our timing calibration and scoring sensitivity analyses address the same concern (Appendix G). KernelBench targets efficient GPU operators and model forward passes, and AlgoTune evaluates numerical solvers through problemsolution interface; both score speedup over reference implementation of selfcontained function (Ouyang et al., 2025; Press et al., 2025). In production, ECO selects code through fleet-wide profiling and checks model-generated performance edits with tests and post-deployment monitoring (Lin et al., 2026). Accelerate Bench instead fixes one complete application workflow for all agents and times it under application-specific correctness constraints; as in SWE-fficiency, agents must first find where runtime is spent, and they may change algorithms, implementations, and build and runtime settings. Long-horizon agent evaluation. RE-Bench is closest in format: agents improve working starting solutions within budgets of up to eight hours, and several of its ML research-engineering tasks score runtime reductions against expert references (Wijk et al., 2025). It normalizes scores between the starting and expert solutions; we report runtime ratios to the provided baseline and verify final submissions on private inputs. AlphaEvolve improves programs through model-proposed edits scored by automated evaluators (Novikov et al., 2025). ALE-Bench evaluates iterative algorithm engineering through public testing and final private evaluation (Imajuku et al., 2025). AutoLab studies sustained improvement of working implementations, and MLS-Bench tests whether improvements to ML components generalize across settings and scales (Xu et al., 2026a; Lyu et al., 2026). Accelerate Bench applies this iterative loop to application-level optimization and records the candidates, timings and feedback behind each result. Scientific coding benchmarks. SciCode evaluates scientific reasoning and code synthesis, while ScienceAgentBench asks agents to implement data-driven tasks from research publications (Tian et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025). AInsteinBench evaluates development in scientific repositories; SWE-bench Science covers scientific software repair and integration (Duston et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2026b). Accelerate Bench starts from working applications and asks agents to accelerate the prescribed computations, subject to constraints on numerical outputs and workflow behavior. 7. Limitations Task coverage and baselines. The evaluation covers CPU workflows at the specified scales and resource budgets. Speedups are relative to task-provided baselines with varying degrees of tuning; they measure improvement from those starting points. Some speedups exploit structure in the specified workload, such as the HPCG-derived operator, which admits direct solver; the tasks measure whether agents find and realize such opportunities, and results at other scales, on other hardware, and in production environments require separate evaluation. 11 Accelerate Bench: Application-Level Program Optimization Agent and execution settings. As in other agent benchmarks, each result reflects model running in its harness, so score differences combine model capability with harness behavior, inference compute, and execution conditions. Every agent receives the same task container, resource and time limits, and timing and correctness rules, and scores are runtime ratios to the task baseline. Table 1 reports one run per agent, and repeated runs cover two agents (Appendix A.3). Separating models from harnesses and measuring sensitivity to hardware placement are natural extensions that the retained programs and containers support. Benchmark versions. Results of v1.0 and v1.1 are reported separately and never combined; v1.1 revised the task statements and fixed several verifier, timing and environment problems (Appendix A). The trajectory analyses use v1.0 runs. Trajectory samples. The trajectory analyses cover five agents. Source labels combine model-assisted annotation with targeted source checks, and prevalence estimates rest on reviewed samples. Version histories cover 31 runs in seven applications, most candidates have one timing observation, and controlled experiments establish effects for the tested artifacts, workloads, and settings. 8. Conclusion Accelerate Bench evaluates application-level optimization on 32 workload-defined CPU tasks with public feedback and private verification. On benchmark v1.1, most programs of the 16 agents are correct, and the size of the speedup separates the agents: the best reaches Score@1 of 67.4% in one run, and the two leading agents are at least 2 faster on 22 or more tasks, the others on 8 to 17. In the analyzed v1.0 runs, computation or reuse changes appear in 225 of 476 labeled runs, compiler and build tuning in only 40, yet controlled replays show that gains depend on build and runtime settings and on other code changes: identical source runs from 0.29 to 2.12, one code change is worth 1.01 or 6.4 depending on another, and in an estimated 52% of analyzed runs, tool output shows such dependency affecting an optimizations speed or correctness. 12 Accelerate Bench: Application-Level Program Optimization

sections.title: Reproducibility Statement
sections.content: Evaluation metrics, run-inclusion and aggregation rules, task resources, and model configurations are described in Section 3 and Appendices DG; Appendix lists the data snapshot behind each result. Each score is stored with its task and verifier versions, the scored program, and the execution settings; process analyses use retained trajectories and evaluator responses. Reproduction requires the same workload definitions, task and verifier versions, execution resources, and agent settings. We will release the versioned task packages, including public tests and verifiers, with the published version of the paper.

sections.title: AI Use Statement
